newsitem.title: USA: Cold seen not damaging U.S. HRW wheat next week.
newsitem.headline: Cold seen not damaging U.S. HRW wheat next week.

text.p: A blast of bitter cold air expected to chill the U.S. High Plains next week will probably not cause much damage to the U.S. hard red winter wheat crop, agaronomists said Friday.

Forecasters said a winter storm system will move through the area next week, bringing several inches of snow to Kansas and Oklahoma. Cold temperatures will follow, dropping temperatures down to the single digits Fahrenheit.
But experts said the wintry conditions will not pose a threat to the newly planted wheat -- and in some cases may actually help the crop.
Agronomists said the forecast for snow bodes well for the crop, since snow will help insulate the wheat plant against severe cold temperatures that can cause winterkill.

"Even if we don't get the snow cover... we have such good growth and such good soil moisture that I wouldn't anticipate any problems at all with the wheat crop," said Kim Anderson, wheat specialist at Oklahoma State University.
"It will possibly be beneficial because it will put the wheat into dormancy and you won't be using up your moisture and your nutrients -- they'll be there next year," Anderson said.
He added that the cold temperatures may even help kill off leaf rust, a potentially damaging fungal disease that has become widespread in the newly-planted HRW wheat crop.
Experts said leaf rust will not damage wheat yields and quality unless it manages to "overwinter" -- that is, survive the winter months and become a problem during the spring.
"(The cold) is going to kill any rust or insect infestation that happens to be bothering the wheat right now," Anderson said.
But others were not so sure that the low temperatures would immediately kill off the rust.

Merle Eversmeyer, research plant pathologist with the U.S. Agriculture Department's Agricultural Research Service in Manhattan, Kan., said he expected next week's weather will have little effect on both the crop and the fungus.
He explained that it usually takes a few cycles of winter weather followed by warm-ups to destroy the rust.
"Right now I don't see much change in the situation. The wheat still looks good and the rust looks fairly healthy, I'm sorry to say," Eversmeyer said.
